content: Solitary lymphatic nodules are anatomical structures located within the small and large intestines. In the small intestine, these nodules are dispersed throughout the mucous membrane, with the highest concentration found in the lower portion of the ileum. Their free surfaces are covered by rudimentary villi, except at their summits. Each nodule is surrounded by the openings of intestinal glands. Structurally, they are composed of densely interwoven retiform tissue, which is tightly packed with lymphocytes and permeated by an extensive capillary network. The spaces within the retiform tissue are continuous with larger lymphatic spaces that encircle the nodule, allowing communication with the lacteal system. These nodules are located partially within the submucosal tissue and partially within the mucous membrane, where they form slight projections into the epithelial layer. In the large intestine, solitary lymphatic nodules are most abundant in the cecum and the vermiform appendix, although they are irregularly scattered throughout the remainder of the intestine. Their structure and organization are similar to those found in the small intestine.
